items.english: I do not know where Ana is.
items.explanation: An indirect question uses no question marks here, but dónde retains its accent.

closerLook.title: Inside a longer sentence
closerLook.body: Si puedes, ¿me llamas? places the opening mark after the initial condition. Punctuation marks the scope of the question rather than automatically enclosing every preceding word.

closerLook.title: More than punctuation
closerLook.body: Writing marks cannot replace the right verb form or word choice. In speech, listeners rely on the structure and intonation instead.

mistakes.explanation: Written direct questions use an opening mark too.
Do not add a full stop after a closing question mark ending the sentence.

practice.prompt: Punctuate: Dónde vives
practice.explanation: Add both marks and retain the accent.

practice.prompt: Punctuate a greeting to Ana followed by Are you coming?: Ana vienes
practice.explanation: The name is outside the question; the comma marks direct address.

practice.prompt: Does No sé dónde está need question marks as a statement?
practice.explanation: It contains an indirect question, with an accent on dónde.

takeaways: Use opening and closing marks for direct questions and exclamations.
Place the opening mark where that part begins.
Indirect questions can keep accents without question marks.

se.bigIdea: Se is a small word with several grammatical jobs. Instead of assigning it one translation, identify the construction around it: self-directed action, a general statement, an affected person, or a pronoun combination.
se.goal: Distinguish four common se patterns using meaning and agreement.

build.title: Look for a self-directed action
build.body: Ana se lava means Ana washes herself. Se links the receiver of the action to Ana. Some verbs with se have a broader or changed meaning, such as irse.

build.title: Look for a general or passive-like statement
build.body: Se vive bien aquí means people live well here: impersonal se with a singular verb. Se venden libros is passive-like: books are sold, with plural agreement.

build.title: Check neighboring pronouns
build.body: In Se lo doy, se replaces le or les before lo/la/los/las. In Se me cayó el vaso, me identifies the affected person, while el vaso controls cayó.

extraExamples.explanation: In this passive-like construction, plural casas agrees with venden.
Se replaces le before lo; it does not mean herself.

items.explanation: Impersonal se has no expressed subject; vive stays singular.
Passive-like se has plural libros as the grammatical subject, so use venden.

closerLook.title: An affected-person pattern
closerLook.body: Se me cayó el vaso means I dropped the glass / the glass fell on me. Caerse describes the event; me marks the affected person. The construction can downplay agency without guaranteeing an accident.

closerLook.title: A personal object stays singular in the impersonal pattern
closerLook.body: Se busca a los responsables uses a personal object with a, not a plural subject; busca stays singular. Contrast Se buscan empleados, where empleados agrees with buscan.

mistakes.explanation: Le/les changes to se before lo/la/los/las.
In this passive-like construction, casas is plural and controls the verb.

practice.prompt: Classify Ana se lava.
practice.explanation: Ana does the washing and receives it.

practice.prompt: Complete: Se __ libros. (vender, passive-like)
practice.explanation: Plural libros requires plural agreement.

practice.prompt: Why does le become se in Se lo doy?
practice.explanation: This se is a pronoun replacement, not a reflexive marker.

takeaways: Identify the construction before translating se.
Impersonal and passive-like patterns differ in agreement.
Se can replace le/les or occur in affected-person constructions.

hypotheticals.bigIdea: Conditional sentences connect a possible situation with its result. Spanish changes the verb pattern depending on whether the condition is treated as open, imagined or contrary to a completed past.
hypotheticals.goal: Distinguish open conditions, imagined present/future conditions and unreal past conditions.

build.title: Leave a possibility open
build.body: Si tengo tiempo, iré means if I have time, I will go. The si clause uses present indicative, even though the situation concerns the future.

build.title: Imagine a different present or future
build.body: Si tuviera tiempo, iría means if I had time, I would go. Use imperfect subjunctive in the condition and conditional in the result.

build.title: Imagine a different completed past
build.body: Si hubiera tenido tiempo, habría ido means if I had had time, I would have gone. Use pluperfect subjunctive for the condition and conditional perfect for the result.

extraExamples.spanish: Si llueve, nos quedaremos en casa.
extraExamples.english: If it rains, we will stay at home.
extraExamples.explanation: An open future possibility uses present llueve after si and future in the result.

extraExamples.english: If I had studied, I would have passed.
extraExamples.explanation: The speaker imagines a different completed past, using compound forms.

items.english: If I have time, I will go.
items.explanation: The condition is treated as open.

items.english: If I had time, I would go.
items.explanation: The speaker takes a more hypothetical stance toward having time.

closerLook.title: Form the imperfect subjunctive
closerLook.body: Start with the preterite ellos form, remove -ron and add -ra endings: tuvieron → tuviera. The -se series, such as tuviese, is also standard.

closerLook.title: Results can vary
closerLook.body: Si tienes tiempo, ven uses a command as the result. Si tengo tiempo, voy can use the present. Mixed-time hypotheticals also exist; choose a pattern by meaning rather than memorizing one mandatory result tense.

mistakes.explanation: An ordinary open future condition uses present indicative after si.
This imagined-condition pattern uses imperfect subjunctive in the si clause.

practice.prompt: Complete an open condition: Si __ tiempo, iré. (tener, yo)
practice.explanation: Use present indicative for an open future condition.

practice.prompt: Complete an imagined condition: Si tuviera tiempo, __. (go, yo)
practice.explanation: The result uses the conditional in this pattern.

practice.prompt: Complete the unreal past: Si hubiera estudiado, __ aprobado.
practice.explanation: Habría + participle builds the conditional perfect result.

takeaways: Decide how the speaker frames the condition.
Open: si + present; imagined: si + imperfect subjunctive.
Unreal past commonly combines hubiera + participle with habría + participle.
